The Serbs who were taken prisoner at Bradina put together a list of what they -- each of them had in terms of weapons. On that list there was also the name of Slobodan Zelenovic. When we asked Slobodan where his rifle was, he said that he left his rifle in Bradina. Myself, together with the military police of the HVO, which came to the command post in Podorasac, we went to Bradina, and we found the rifle in the house of Vaso Kuljanin. Slobodan was at home up until the day when the military police took all the Serbs to the command post in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that the police took all the Serbs from Celebici, did all the Serbs remain in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: When we conduct the negotiations about the surrender of weapons for Serbs, stated that they would surrender weapons, and they did so. They surrendered them to me directly. However, when Zvonko Zovko ordered that all Serbs come to the command post in Podorasac, by mistake these four men also went there, the four that had surrendered weapons. When I learned about this, I went to the Celebici prison and submitted a request to the commission which was at Celebici to release the four men who had surrendered weapons. The commission considered the request and within an hour released the four individuals who were taken there by mistake. Those persons were Dragan Zivak, son of Mirka. Mirko Zivak, son of Vase. Slavko Zivak, son of Vase, and Nikola Stojanovic. Two of these four individuals continued to be in Brdani to date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned here that you contacted the commission there. Do you know any members there? Do you know who were the members there whom you saw in the commission?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: The members of the commission were Goran Lokas, Kostic Stenek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those who you saw?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mehmedalija Rizvic and Mirsad Subasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am Edina Residovic, and I am Defence Counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. I am going to ask you several questions. During the examination in chief you said that your unit, which belonged to the Zuconik (phonetic) detachment, took part in the combat operations involving the liberation of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Ramic, can you tell me who was your commander during those operations?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: During those operations my commander was Zvonko Zovko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, if I were to tell you that Zvonko Zovko during the entire operations of the liberation of Bradina was the commander in charge of the entire combat operations of the liberation of Bradina, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, after Bradina was liberated, is it true that your unit, along with other members of the Territorial Defence, undertook search of the entire area of the Bradina village?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes. Part of my unit did conduct a search and also secured the freedom of movement of the civilian defence, which was in the village of Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In light of that fact, Mr. Ramic, can you testify before this Trial Chamber that part -- this part of your unit was finding numerous pieces of weapon in that area in the next month or so?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes. I can testify to that, that even a month and a month and a half later pieces of weaponry were being found in the village of Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, is it also true that members of the investigative commission, with which you communicated on one occasion regarding your fellow citizens and to which Mr. Kostic, Mr. Subasic belonged, did ask you to go to a specific place and to collect some weapons from it?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes. The commission did ask me personally to go, along with them and the police. In other words, to take them to the location where some weapons might be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true that you did find weapons there?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true, Mr. Ramic, that in certain situations the person who owned this weapon would occasionally also go to that location?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes. It happened on several occasions, that if I or the military police was unable to find the weapons, based on the description of the person who owned it, this person would then come with the police escort to show precisely where that weapon was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, you answered my previous question by saying that part of your unit did provide secure -- the secure freedom of movement. Would you agree with me if I said that after the liberation of Bradina the citizens who remained there, in other words, individuals who were not taken to Celebici, women and others, had absolute freedom of movement, both in that area, in other areas?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with you on that. They did move about freely, both in Bradina and outside of Bradina. We kept a log. Members of my unit kept a log detailing the movement, movements, and we took down exactly who went where and when, and when did they come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, is it true that these persons could freely come to Brdani, where you were, based on the logbook which you kept in Konjic, and could come to see the members of their families who were detained either in Celebici or at Musala?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, they could move about freely either go to Brdani, to Konjic, to Celebici, to see their family members. I would take, would drive these persons on many occasions from Bradina to Brdani because it was on my way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, is it true that you know that the civilian protection of these civilians was also organised, and that the civilian protection also cared about security of these people?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes. I know that there was civilian protection staff, and this staff did take care of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, since the M17 highway had been opened and refugees from other parts of our country moved through that route, was it true that both you and other members of the TO, when asked by the citizens, did provide security for these people, either their own security or security of their property?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes. Any time we received such requests, we would show up to provide protection, if it was needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, is it true that the citizens of your village, Brdani, as well as the villages of Bradina, had a possibility to go and visit their family members at Celebici and bring them food and clothing?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Every other day they had a right to go to Celebici to take food and clothing. I frequently talked to the persons who were going there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, have you ever heard -- did you ever hear of any mistreatment of people or something similar as going on in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No, never. A moment ago I mentioned that I spoke to these persons frequently, that I would give them rides to Konjic or back to Brdani, things like that, but, in any event, I never heard that any one of them had any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, is it true that certain Serbian families, even though Brdani had a majority Muslim population, stayed the entire war together with you and lived with you?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, 30 percent of the Serbian population remained in Brdani and lived there, and they lived in Brdani to date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, there was an incident in Brdani, however, and it involved a Serbian family. Do you know whether somebody was killed in Brdani?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately. I know that the Draganic family with three members perished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, do you know whether an investigation was conducted about this case and whether persons who were suspected of this act were prosecuted, and if you know, when was it? When did this take place?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember this. This was in late January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean '93?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: '93. I apologise. Yes, it was in '93. It was in '93. I had just come out of the hospital. I was at home with my father, at my father's, and early in the morning I was awakened by my neighbour, that is the neighbour of the Draganic family. Since I was the only person who had a telephone in the village, he told me about this incident and he asked me to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that, you know, that the MUP commission did come and conduct an investigation on this matter?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I was going to say, that the police did come out and conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, this last question. What happened to you and how long were you in the hospital, and why?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I had a traffic accident. I was in a military vehicle. It was a serious accident. I broke my hip, fractured my hip and four ribs, and I was on crutches for the next two or threes months

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, thank you very much. I have no further questions. Your Honours, this concludes my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we'll have to adjourn 'til 2.30 p.m., when we'll continue with other cross-examination. The Trial Chamber will now rise. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.03 p.m. 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness is on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe I am next in line, the Defence of Mr. Mucic has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may question from here, I only have one witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are free.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examined by Ms. McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Ramic, we had an opportunity to speak briefly at the break earlier today, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the record, I am Cynthia McMurrey, I am the counsel for Esad Landzo. We had talked about, as Ms. Residovic had asked you, that the families of the detainees, especially the detainees from Brdani, they were able to come and bring food and clean clothes to the detainees at Celebici, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, from your personal knowledge, you know that the wives of many of the detainees and you know that about the ones from Brdani were able to visit with their husbands in Celebici, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, three times a week. They were allowed to visit their family to bring food and clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to put a time on this, the people from Brdani were brought to Celebici sometime at the first day of June or maybe the last day of May, and from the first time that they arrived in Celebici, the families were able to bring food and clothing and have visitation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I personally spoke to people who visited the prison and that means that there were people from Brdani there too. And I spoke to them personally. And I said that sometimes I took them along to Konjic, from Konjic to Brdani.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ramic, and thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mrs. McHenry, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed. Cross-examined by Ms. McHenry:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you stated that you were a commander of an independent platoon that belonged to the TO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Correct. At the beginning this was the Territorial Defence, and later, detachment was organised and I belonged to this detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you wear a uniform with TO insignia?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when were you commander of that, the unit, from when to when, approximately?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: In mid-April, up until the end of July, when I was sent to become the assistant commander of the detachment. At the time when commanders Zvonko Zovko went over to HVO. At that time, a new commander was determined and I became this new commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it your testimony, sir, that from mid-April until the end of July, Mr. Zovko Zvonko was a member of the TO or a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Zovko Zvonko was a member of the -- he was my commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What period? What period was he a commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From mid-April and I can't remember correctly up until what point he was my commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you're aware, aren't you, that Mr. Zovko was a member of the HVO from mid-April forward; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I don't know, I can't remember. I know that he was my commander. But that was probably a general command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your testimony, sir, that you cannot remember whether or not for all of May, June and July, Mr. Zovko Zvonko was a member of the HVO or not?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I was -- I belonged to an independent, platoon I was at Brdani, and I was blocked off, and that's why I belonged to an independent platoon. And I know that I received orders from Zvonko Zovko and whether that was a joint command or whether it belonged to HVO or TO, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you don't know whether or not your superior, Mr. Zovko Zvonko, was a member of the HVO or not, did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was a member of HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now when you say you were a member of an independent platoon, that doesn't mean that you weren't a member of the TO, correct?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: It is correct that I belong -- that I was a member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so, is it, you would -- is it possible that as a member of the TO, your superior was a member of the HVO, was that kind of reporting normal at this time in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I don't know whether Zovko Zvonko belonged to the TO and if he did whether it was a joint command or whether he belonged to the HVO. I really don't know that and I cannot remember that. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember that he wore a red checker board as his insignia?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I can't remember. I think he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that insignia normally signifies someone who is a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it your testimony that you do not know what insignia members of the HVO normally wore?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I know what insignia they wore, but I cannot remember what Zvonko Zovko had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the beginning when you were head of your platoon -- your unit, I'm sorry, starting from mid-April, did anyone appoint you to that position or was it just part of your own creation?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I was appointed by the staff of the Territorial Defence and by the recommendation of the villagers of Brdani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive your appointment in writing?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Zovko Zvonko sign your appointment?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I can't remember who signed it, but I did have it in writing. I think that it was signed by some Boric, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you agree with me that in the very beginning parts of the war, April, May, June, for instance, there was some confusion, including about the TO and the HVO and lines of authority?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Could you explain to me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you don't seem to know certain things, such as whether or not your superior was a member of the HVO or TO. And I am asking whether or not there was some confusion at the time about the various entities and lines of authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I object. The witness said he doesn't know whether it was HVO or the joint command, but he didn't say that there was some misunderstandings or confusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not so sure who is in on this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not too sure who is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's Mr. Karabdic's witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know other colleagues also made objections if the witness said something before when I had my witnesses. I did not notice that this was unusual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is unusual.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then I apologise. I apologise again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Actually was what he said was that he did not remember, not that there was any confusion. That's what he said. He doesn't remember, whether he belonged to HVO or TO or to joint command, Mr. Zovko. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, was there any confusion in the beginning stages of the war about such things as what entities and lines of authority?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible that as a member of the TO your superior, Mr. Zovko Zvonko, could have been a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I said earlier that I was separated, I was separated and I belonged to TO and I know that my commander was Zvonko Zovko. It was a very long time ago. I can't remember every detail. But -- and I also cannot remember whether he was a member of HVO, TO, but I do know that he was my commander and that I received all my orders from him. And I belonged to the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that during this period of time, both the TO and the HVO were active in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, they were active.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when the TO and the HVO did not agree?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I remember a joint command and then later HVO and TO separated and the army of BH was created and HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you understand his position now?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you stated that Mr. Zovko Zvonko was in charge of the operation in Brdani, do you mean that he was in charge of all the troops who participated in the operation of Brdani?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Zvonko Zovko was the most responsible person for that area and for the operation around Brdani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you say he was the most responsible, do you mean, do you know whether or not he was in charge of all the troops who participated in the Brdani operation?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, he was in charge and I personally -- and I remember when he called us before the operation, he called us, or the commanders, where he gave us instructions and orders and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, during that operation, he was in charge of all the TO troops, all the MUP troops and all the HVO troops that participated in that operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I don't know about the police, but as far as HVO and TO, yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated that the Serbs did not take part in the mobilisation at the beginning of the war; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: The Serbs did not take part in the mobilisation of TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did that mobilisation take place, were there letters written, was it just up to who volunteered, how exactly did the mobilisation take place?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: The mobilisation started from around the 15th of April, 1992, and both Muslims and Serbs were supposed to be mobilised, but the Serbs did not mobilise, actually the entire population was supposed to be mobilised, but the Serbs did not want to take part in the mobilisation effort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, sir, is, how did the mobilisation take place? How were people informed where they should report to such and such a place to be mobilised? Or, was it just up to the person's own initiative?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No, it was not up to their own initiative, but through the staff of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, do you have any information whatsoever about whether -- how people were informed, that they should be mobilised or should report somewhere for purposes of mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: For example, I was one of the representatives of the Village of Brdani. And in this body, there were also people of Serbian ethnic background. So that from the headquarters of the Territorial Defence, we received some instructions, but right after the very beginning, there was a conflict. It started from the demand to set up joint guards. It had to do with the negotiations, but the Serbs refused negotiations and the joint guards. And after that they refused the surrender of weapons and the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you stated that as part of the negotiations, the Serbs were told that they should either become members of the TO or if they didn't want to become members, they should give up their weapons. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember all those negotiations and meetings. And the demand was to join the mobilisation. And those who did not want to do so, were responsible to surrender their weapons, for which there was no authorisation to carry them. However --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: However, the Serbs refused both and they said that -- so they refused mobilisation, and they said that if they have to surrender their weapons, we will have war, which happened eventually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, if a Serb then did not have any weapons, that person was not required to become a member of the TO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: They could if they wanted to, but they didn't have to. It was important. The most important thing were the weapons for which there was no authorisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned joint guards, a second ago, can you explain to me what you mean by "joint guards"?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: The Muslims saw that Serbs have a lot of weapons. And the Serbs had the story that they were scared of some attacks. And then we suggested that if they were scared, and we saw that they had the weapons, we suggested that we should together keep guard to -- during the night, to protect both houses of Serbs and Croats. However, they refused that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly during your direct, after the negotiations, there were some Serbs who either joined the TO or gave up their weapons and that there were other Serbs who did not agree and were part of the Chetnik forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes. A lot of Serbs who surrendered their weapons -- actually four Serbs -- there were only four Serbs who surrendered their weapons voluntarily. Everybody else took their weapons to shoot against the inhabitants of the Village of Brdani. All those who used their weapons had to surrender them after that. Some of them were captured, but, however, those who did not have any weapons were left in peace and they could move freely just like anybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say those who did not have those weapons, according to your testimony, you're just referring the those four people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No, there were more people who did not have any weapons at all and who still live in Brdani today and who had spent the entire war there who wanted to join the TO did so and we have an example where a Serb joined the army and he remained in the army up until the last day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say that there were some other Serbs who were part of the Chetnik forces, what do you mean when you say "Chetnik forces"?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Those are the forces -- for me, they are those forces who did not even want to negotiate, those people who I mentioned earlier, who during the last negotiations were already up in the hills, who only wanted to see war happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Chetnik forces have any connection with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I think -- I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated that there was an order from Mr. Zvonko Zovko, that all persons who had weapons or who participated in the fighting in Brdani should report the a command post, were you the person who received that order from Mr. Zovko?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: One morning, Zvonko Zovko, through the security officer, informed the Serbian population, who had some weapons and who were involved in the operation in Brdani, that they should come, that they should come to the command post in Podorasac and this is what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my question is, who actually received this order from Mr. Zovko?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: The security officer received it and I was also made aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is the security officer?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Nehir Pavo (Phon).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you would agree with me that you were one of the persons who implemented that order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was it the case that this order for Mr. Zovko was just communicated and there was some kind of honour system where the Serbs just turned themselves in?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No, I just knew about this order, but the security officer had a higher rank than me and he was the one who fulfilled this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "fulfilled this order," do you mean went around and arrested people?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Not arrested. After the fall of Brdani, they lived freely, normally in Brdani up until this order. And after this order they had to go to Podorasac and they were free at that time. And in Podorasac, a truck was waiting for them, which took them to the prison at Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, according to your understanding, people were free to go to Podorasac, or not to go, it was just up to the individual person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is not what he said. They were all there, not that it was up to them whether to go or not. He hadn't said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He said they were free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They were free to go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they free not to go? Were they free not to go to Podorasac?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No, no, they were ordered to go to Podorasac. And those who were not at homes at that point in time when he was making the rounds in the village, they were taken in the evening or the next morning. That means that they had to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that you told people that they were required to go there. You went around to various houses and various people and told persons that they had to go to Podorasac, correct?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No, it is not. I did not do that. Mr. Spago Nedzad was a security officer and went from house to house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never informed any person about any -- you never informed any Serb person about this order at all? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: The order was received by the officer and following this order he went to Brdani and he informed the villagers. And this all happened within an hour, because Brdani is about a kilometre or two away from Podorasac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your testimony is you had nothing to do with this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with it because the Serbs turned in their weapons. They did not want to join the TO. And they didn't bother me without weapons, as such. They were not a threat to the village, so they were able to continue to move about freely, like the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many men from Brdani were taken to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Somewhere around 50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated that Mr. Slobodan Zelenovic had a weapon. How do you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: The Serbs, who compiled the list of who owned what, contained the name of Slobodan Zelenovic. And after the fall of Bradina, he returned to Brdani, and when we asked him to turn in the weapons, when we asked him where it was, because his colleagues told us that he had some, then he told us that the weapons, that the weapons were in Bradina. And later they were found. And also Slobodan Zelenovic's father said that he -- that he had given his weapons to his son, Sloboran (Phon).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the father say that to you?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, he said it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Together with Zvonko Zovko, I was present when the weapons were recovered. So that was after the fall of Bradina, when part of the Serbs who had been disarmed was taken. And those who were able to go back home, who had not been arrested -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I am going to ask that you listen to my question very carefully and that you only answer my question, please. When was it that Mr. Zelenovic's father --

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: After the fall of Bradina, when the weapons were being surrendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this before or after Mr. Zelenovic was taken to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: This happened before Mr. Zelenovic went to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see this list yourself that was compiled?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs compiled a list and we had this list. I had it and Zvonko Zovko and I don't know who else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is this list now?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Later on I took the weapons to the command post in Podorasac, and a list went along with it, and I believe that it ended up there. And it was -- the turning in of the weapons was taken down in the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have a copy of that report?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there was a time that Mr. Rajko Draganic surrendered a weapon to you, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Rajko Draganic. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this. Do you remember taking Mr. Draganic's car away from him?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic's car was taken by the TO for its own use, and it was done together with the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were involved in taking Mr. Draganic's car, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No. It was the police. Mr. Draganic had a car which was a Yugo make and he had given it to a friend, so the car was not in his possession. And I remember that there was a TO order that this car be taken for the use of the TO. I remember that he had several cars and that there were -- they were taken for the use of the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were commander of the TO unit in Brdani, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, but Rajko Draganic lived closer to Podorasac than to Brdani. He was just born in Brdani and his father lives up there, but he built a house much closer to Podorasac than to Brdani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me move forward. You indicated, if I understood you correctly, that you went to Celebici to see about getting four people who had been wrongly imprisoned released. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was this, approximately?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: That day, when I received information that the people who had surrendered the weapons upon request were also taken to Celebici. When I learned that, I went to Celebici and I submitted request in writing to the commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you to just listen to my question. If you don't know the answer to my question, you can just say, "I don't know." My question was: When was it, approximately, that you went to Celebici to get these four persons released?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I believe that it was on that or the following day. So I can't tell you whether it was on that day or the following one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it have been in the end of May or beginning of June, sir?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I believe it was in early June. I believe it was in early June, but the day when all the Serbs were taken from Brdani, that is when those four were also taken. I believe that it was on that day that I went to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many times did you go to Celebici in all?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you indicated that you saw Mr. Lokas in Celebici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I saw him, but whether it was the first or the second time, I don't remember that. But I did see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Who else did you see -- besides the commission members, did you know anyone else who worked in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I saw the guards. I saw security on that occasion when I came there. I saw the military police, the police, the guards. I was at the gate while all this was going on regarding this request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any guards who worked in Celebici at any time?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the names of those guards?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I knew the members of the then MUP. I knew Dzajic, I knew Hazim Delalic. In fact, I saw him at that time. It was a long time ago, and it's a detail to recall all the persons whom I saw there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guard that you know named Mr. Dzajic, what is his first name and his nickname, if you have one?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I don't know his first name, and I only know him as Dzajic. I have -- I did not spend much time in Konjic, in fact, and I did not know these people very well. I knew them by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Hazim Delic doing when you saw him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I saw Hazim Delic, he was a HVO policeman. I remember him being on crutches at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, if you can't remember what your own superior was, how is it that you remember that Mr. Delic was a HVO police officer?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Even later Mr. Delic, along with another few police officers, came to Brdani and Bradina to the checkpoint, with or without persons who were in detention, looking for weapons. Part of my platoon was in Brdani, part was in Bradina, so that I was constantly shuttling back and forth. And those days we were involved in search of weapons, so I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Delic wear HVO insignia?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Delic. I am not sure whether he wore any insignia, but at that time there was no TO police, so he could only have been a HVO police officer. There was the MUP police force and the HVO police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you talk to Mr. Delic about what his role was in the camp, or the fact that he was a military police officer?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No, I never talked to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it you know that Mr. Delic was a military police officer at that time?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I know because he had a white belt on just like his colleagues did, and I know that he took part in this search for weapons. I know that he would come to search for them with or without persons who were in detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you remember that every time you saw him he had a white belt; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: It was when I saw the camp to Celebici for the first time, and on later occasions -- I am not sure that he had it on every time, but I remember the first time he did, and maybe later on too. The police had their own uniforms and the belts, the white belts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Delic manning the gate when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No, he was up there somewhere near the administration building, and I remember well that he was on crutches, so I was a bit -- so I was wondering a little bit why he was on crutches. I remember that detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he just walking around or was he standing guard outside the building, or just what was it that he was doing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No, I don't know what he was doing. I was standing at the gate and he was standing inside. What he was doing, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was standing inside, meaning you saw him through a window, sir?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No, no, no. I saw him from the gate. He was at the administration building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he standing still or was he walking around?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: He was walking on crutches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see Mr. Mucic at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Never. I was only there three times and I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other two times you were in Celebici, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: The second time it was the oath giving, and there was another subsequent time I was on duty as assistant commander for logistics. And inside the compound was a weapons specialist, that is a person who repaired weapons. We had several rifles that had been broken, so I was using him to repair them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the person repairing weapons, was that a prisoner or was it a soldier, TO soldier, or some other kind of soldier?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: It was a soldier who was a member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in Celebici or Musala you went several times and saw some detainees, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: When I came for the weapons, I saw a number of detainees inside the area where they were kept. That is, I saw a part of them. The door was wide open, it was high summer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point in Celebici or Musala did you see Sreten Zelenovic?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No, never in Celebici, and I never went to Musala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever indicate to any detainees that you could help get them released if they would pay money?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: I personally did not need to go to the prison. I had no contact with the guards, I had no contact with the commission, who was the only authority that could release the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Did you hear the question? Counsel asked whether you could assist them for a fee.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you stated that family members were allowed to go visit Celebici and visit the prisoners. Is that from the very -- is it the case that that is from the time that -- the very first time that Celebici was opened?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Yes, they could visit their family members from the very beginning to take them -- to bring them food and clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your testimony is they could visit the prisoners every other day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Three times a week he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, three times a week.

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: Three times a week. That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you ever at Celebici when anyone was allowed to see one of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Zaim Cosic
utterances.text: No. I was there three times altogether. The first time, as I already said, I came to -- for those four. That was the day when they had been detained, or the next day. The second time it was for the oath taking, and the third time when I brought those weapons. But I gave a ride a number of times to the people who went there. These were my neighbours, male and female. I would take them to Konjic or, if I went beyond Konjic, to Celebici also.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination? Mr. Karabdic, any re-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: My colleague, Tom Moran and I, have made an agreement that he would examine the next witness, so I need to call him. But as far as this witness is concerned, no, I do not have any further questions of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran is here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is just in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was watching on television, so I knew I would be right on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have no questions. Thank you very much, sir. You are discharged now. May we have the next witness. You can leave now. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while they are bringing him in, I just thought I would tell you a few housekeeping things that we -- some scheduling things. We have delivered to the registry a package of documents which we are planning on introducing. We've asked the registry to pre-mark them. So if we run out of witnesses, the reason is so that the registry, at its convenience, can mark these documents rather than all of us sitting here while 183 documents are marked. I believe you can see them directly in front of you, Judge Odio-Benito. I believe you are looking at them. Those will come in tomorrow through Amira Klaric. She is number four on our list. Also I have another witness that is waiting after this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your next witness, Emir Dzajic, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The next witness we have is Mr. Djacic, and then Ms. Klaric is number four on the list. But because of the pre-marking, we thought that it would be more convenient for all concerned if we waited until the registry had everything marked and then just bring her in. She is a custodian of record. Since she can explain how the records are kept and what they are. And that's all of the knowledge she has about this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I thought it would be much more convenient for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Swear the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may sit down, please Examined by Mr. Moran

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Emir Dzajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dzajic, where are you from?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: From Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you still reside in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Konjic municipality in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you employed, sir?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I am a driver with the Federation Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what is your rank in the Federation Army, sir?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Sergeant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in May and June, July and August of 1992, how were you employed?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I was a driver with the MUP in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, in May of 1992, in fact on May the 20th of 1992, did your unit take part in any military activity around the Village of Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other military formations taking part in these military operations with you, sir?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: The HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, at this time did the TO have any military police or were all of the military policemen part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Only the HVO part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you and your comrades first arrived in Donje Selo -- first, how did you get there? Did you march in or did you take vehicles or how did you get there?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: By vehicles. Vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was one of those vehicles equipped with a loud speaker?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that loud speaker used to summon someone, asking them to come out?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that? Do you know, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Osman Novalic from the MUP of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was using the loud speaker to ask someone to come out and surrender; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was he looking for?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Lazar Cecez. Since they worked together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they worked together, were they both in the MUP, or was he a traffic policeman, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, which is it? Was he a member of MUP or was he a traffic policeman?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: He was about 10 to 15 days before that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which one, sir? Was he a traffic policeman or was he in MUP?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: He was a traffic policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you very much. Do you know why Mr. Osman was causing Lazar Cecez to come out?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: To surrender the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there was information that Mr. Cecez had weapons?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did Lazar Cecez surrender as he was asked or what happened after he was asked to surrender?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Everything would have been fine if he had surrendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that he did not surrender, sir?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time during that day, did your unit receive any fire from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, from the upper side of the railroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, how much was it? Was it just a shot or two or was it a large volume of fire?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: It was a stronger attack, which was prepared before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, who fired the first shots, if you know? Was it the MUP and the police and the HVO or was it the people living in the village?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Probably the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, there will be some disagreement over who is the aggressor. When you say the "aggressor," do you mean the --

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people living in the village?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they had any prepared defensive positions?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see those positions, sir, after the, after the fighting was over with?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: You could see it before and after the shooting. And you could not pass through the main road, M-17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, these positions that were blocking the main road, M-17, based on your experience and training as a sergeant in the Army of the Federation, how long would it take to prepare positions like that? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Of whose positions?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Positions that the Serbs had, the prepared positions on the top of the railroad, was that something that could have been done in the morning, or would it have taken several days to prepare these positions, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: They had enough time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. About how long did this shooting last, sir?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what caused the fighting to die out? Did the one side leave the battle field or did night fall or did everybody run out of ammunition or what?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: We received an order to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, did you go back the next day?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: We returned the same night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you returned that night, was there another battle or what happened then?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: No, there was no new battle. We did a count and we were missing two of our comrades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find them the next day, sir?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, behind the Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what condition were they in?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: In a very ugly condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they alive or dead?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: They were dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you search the area after you found your comrades' bodies?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find any weapons?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We found some medications, some weapons and in two to three stables we found a lot of weapons, Russian weapons, a machine gun, M-53, binoculars, knives, but I would rather say sabres, not knives and metal and steel bats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, did you take any prisoners on either day?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about many prisoners did you take if you recall?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I only remember Snjezana Zivak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to them, sir?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Those who were in the woods and caught there ended in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were abused or beaten by the people that captured them?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't know. I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on that day, were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, I was. My leg was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, by the way, approximately how prisoners, if you know, were captured in the Village of Donje Selo when you were there, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately, roughly? I mean, was it a few or a lot? Or, you know, five or a hundred or a thousand? Just roughly.

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: A few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Sir, after you were wounded, how long were you in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Four to five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you got out of the hospital, how were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I went to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at Celebici, what were your duties, sir?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I was a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by the way, sir, when you were assigned to Celebici, who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Rale Musinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this man sitting behind me with the sunglasses on, that's Pavo Mucic, did you see Pavo at Celebici at all?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man sitting behind me with the sunglasses on is Pavo Mucic, do you know Pavo?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Not very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him very many times while you were at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Once, once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, while you were at Celebici, did you have an occasion to meet a woman named Milojka Antic and her brother, a man named Cedo Antic?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you meet them? How did that occur?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: They were brought to us, to our unit. They were interrogated by the expert commission to say whether they have any weapons or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you present during the interrogation, sir?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I was -- I only brought them to the interrogation room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. By the way, when these people were brought to the interrogation room, were their hands tied or were they beaten or threatened or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Never was anybody beaten or tied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you hear any of the interrogation of either Ms. Antic or her brother?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I was only called to go with them to the Village of Idbar to take the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, that's what I was going to get into next. That's exactly what I wanted to talk about, did you take either Milojka Antic or her brother, Cedo to the village to look for weapons?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it one of them or both of them?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: It was both of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anyone besides you go with them?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: A military policeman of the HVO, Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you got to the village, did you find any weapons?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: We did find a semi-automatic rifle, M-48, at Milojka's under a cherry tree in the garden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who pointed that out to you?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: The brother, for his rifle, on the chicken coop and Ms. Antic under the cherry tree, she did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, so there were two rifles that you found, one --

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you make a report for your superiors about the time --

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time you made that report, were you an experienced report writer, or was this the first report you'd ever done?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: My first report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking back on it, were there some things you'd put in it and some things you might leave out and some things you might do differently?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there some things you left out of the report or some things you wished you put in now or some things that you'd put back in the report back then that you'd wished you left out?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the help of the usher, I have a copy of that document.

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: The differences...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the differences? Okay. Hold on a sec.

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: The differences were that in the first report we did not put in it, his sister, because we thought that there was no need.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "his sister," are you referring to Milojka Antic?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, a document was just placed in front of you, it's Document D/...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Defence document D-26/3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a copy of the report that you made on the 18th day of June in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that your signature down at the bottom or a copy of your signature because this is a copy?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature above yours?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: The signature of Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way did you see Hazim physically sign the original of this document? If you did, you did, if you didn't, you didn't?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You did it together?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, while you were at Celebici, did you have occasion to deal with a women named Grozdana Cecez?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if -- what her relation is to Lazar Cecez?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: No translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what her relationship was to Lazar Cecez? Do you know if they were husband and wife? I am not getting a translation, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, I do, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you engage in any interrogation of Mrs. Cecez at the direction of Rale Musinovic?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you trying to find out?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: We tried to find out things about her husband and other people that we did not find in the lower village with regard to the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you get any useful information from Ms. Cecez?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: She did not want to say anything. She said that she didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your presentation, was she beaten or coerced or threatened in any way to give information?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: No, nobody did it while I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did -- were you ever present at any time when Ms. Cecez was sexually assaulted by anyone?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Never, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have much contact with Ms. Cecez or Ms. Antic during your time as a driver in the camp?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I would bring her food, cigarettes and occasionally and to Grozdana Cecez even flowers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you bring them coffee?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do that on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, on more than one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at any time did either of those two women ever complain to you that they had been sexually assaulted?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: To me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, to you, did they ever tell you that someone had sexually assaulted them?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: While I was there, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Are you familiar with Mr. Delic's -- well, let me back off just a second. When you came to the camp and were first assigned there, that was in what, late May or early June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, when you were first assigned to Celebici after you first got out of the hospital, about when was that, late May or early June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: In early June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your physical condition at the time?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I was wounded. I couldn't move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were you on crutches or --

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, I was helping myself with my healthy foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether Mr. Delic at that time was on crutches?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, he had two crutches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what Mr. Delic's duties were at that time?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: He had none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what did he do with his days? Did he just sit around and drink coffee -- or, I guess in his case, tea. Or did he perform any minor duties around the camp?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: He was doing more sitting than walking around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And he was a member of the HVO military police, you said that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he was an officer?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he just an ordinary policeman?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: He was an ordinary policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he have the authority to issue any orders to you?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, while you were at the camp, were family members permitted to visit their relatives who were incarcerated there?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did that begin, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I know it was done on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it in middle of June, late June or early June, or if you don't recall, you don't recall?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these family members allowed to bring their relatives food or cigarettes or clothing or other things?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that food and clothing was given to them, wasn't it, given to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Masic from Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. There came a time, didn't there, when some members of the TO were assigned to the prison as guards?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember about when that was?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who was in command of those members of the TO?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Sejo Mustafic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a bit about the conditions in the camp, both for the staff and for the inmates. Let's first talk about food, okay. For the last couple of days, you've been living in the Bel Air Hotel down the street, and since I live there too, I have seen the meals you've been eating. Were they eating the same kind of meals we're eating down there?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: They did eat, but not similar meals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about you, were your meals -- what were your meals like?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: The same as theirs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where that food was cooked?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: The city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did that food get to the prisoners, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: By car with a driver, Ustalic Zlatan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ustalic, is that the name?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And was the food tasty or was it plain, what kind of food was it? Tell us a little bit about the food.

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Whatever it was, what could you do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there often bread with it?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, and if you don't know, that's fine, whether the prisoners got the same amount of food that you got?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the -- let's talk a little bit about the sleeping facilities. Was the camp crowded?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the prisoners use for toilet facilities; do you know?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they use, sir?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: The inmates from No. 22 used the toilet in the command facility. No. 6 and 9 had outside toilets. And they had a place for them to use. And the ladies who were at the gate had toilet facilities inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the facilities, the outside facilities that you just described, were those what we would call in the military a field toilet?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, field and some toilets were made which were better, but such were the conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they're similar to the kind of field facilities that the army of the federation would use today if you go to the field to train?

utterances.speaker: Emir Dzajic
utterances.text: Yes, we still use such facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have about ten or fifteen minutes. Would this be a convenient point to break? It's a subject chain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, we will take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may sit down. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
